clue.text: A person of promise

parts.note: read as someone who makes promises on another's behalf, the godparent at a christening or the backer who pledges money

explanation.surface: A promising young talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of promise' suggests potential, but here it means someone who makes a promise: a godparent vows on a child's behalf, a backer pledges support.
explanation.definitionFit: A godparent or guarantor is someone who formally undertakes obligations for another.

clue.text: Their users evidently don't appreciate Browning

definitions.text: Their users evidently don't appreciate Browning

parts.words: Their users evidently don't appreciate Browning
parts.note: Browning reads as the poet, but means getting a tan, which these protect against

explanation.surface: Some readers clearly dislike the poetry of Robert Browning.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital B makes 'Browning' look like the Victorian poet, but it is browning from the sun, which people under parasols avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: Parasols and awnings keep off the sun's rays, preventing a tan.

clue.text: The side of the head

parts.note: on a coin, one face carries the monarch's head; the clue reads like part of the skull

explanation.surface: Part of a person's skull, beside the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: It sounds anatomical, like the temple, but the head is the one on a coin: the face bearing it is the 'heads' side.
explanation.definitionFit: On a coin or medal, the principal face, usually bearing a portrait, as opposed to the reverse.

clue.text: Miss Close may be disposed to make breaches of syntax

indicators.note: disposed means arranged, so the letters of the name may be set out differently

explanation.surface: A woman called Miss Close might be inclined to commit grammatical errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disposed to' reads as 'inclined to', but 'disposed' means arranged: rearrange MISS CLOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammatical blunders such as 'between you and I' are errors of usage.

clue.text: A well-known thriller seen in its proper perspective

indicators.note: tells us the answer can be seen sitting inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A celebrated suspense story viewed in a balanced way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in' says the answer sits within 'its proper'. Patrick Hamilton's 1929 murder play, filmed by Hitchcock in 1948, is the thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Hamilton's stage murder play, later a Hitchcock film, named after the cord used to strangle the victim.

clue.text: Lambs go for them, naturally

indicators.note: read as 'in their own free way', telling us these letters are tumbled about

explanation.surface: Young sheep naturally enjoy frisking about.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the letters of LAMBS GO, rearranged as 'naturally' signals, give the frisky leaps lambs make.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful skips and leaps are what young lambs famously do in spring fields.

clue.text: They are sometimes got by waiting

definitions.text: They are sometimes got by waiting

parts.words: They are sometimes got by waiting
parts.note: waiting reads as patience, but means waiting at table, which earns tips

explanation.surface: Patience brings rewards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waiting' sounds like patience, but it is waiting on tables: waiters receive tips.
explanation.definitionFit: Tips are money given for service by restaurant customers.

clue.text: "—— are May when they are ——" (A.Y.L.I.)

parts.note: a quotation from As You Like It with the same word missing at both ends

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's As You Like It about youth.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosalind says in As You Like It: 'men are April when they woo, December when they wed; ___ are May when they are ___, but the sky changes when they are wives.'
explanation.definitionFit: Unmarried young women, compared by Rosalind to the springtime month before marriage.

clue.text: He's interested in one's looks

parts.note: looks reads as appearance, but means looking, the act of seeing

explanation.surface: Someone who notices how a person appears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looks' suggests appearance, but here it means sight: an eye doctor cares how you see.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an eye specialist, who examines vision.

clue.text: One thing one can't look forward to on a sea-cruise

definitions.text: One thing one can't look forward to on a sea-cruise

parts.words: One thing one can't look forward to on a sea-cruise
parts.note: look forward to reads as anticipate, but means literally face ahead toward a ship's rear

explanation.surface: A disappointment on a holiday voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look forward to' means anticipate, but literally: you cannot look forward and see the back of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear part of a vessel lies behind anyone facing the bow.

clue.text: Not the answer to " Tell me the old, old story "

definitions.text: Not the answer to " Tell me the old, old story "

parts.words: Not the answer to " Tell me the old, old story "
parts.note: the hymn asks for a familiar tale; a book whose name means 'new' is precisely what it does not want

explanation.surface: A line from a well-known hymn asking to hear a familiar tale again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tell Me the Old, Old Story' is a Victorian hymn. The answer is a work of fiction whose name also means 'new', so it is the opposite of an old story.
explanation.definitionFit: A long prose fiction takes its name from a word for something fresh and new, the opposite of old.

clue.text: It's said to be dull and commonplace

definitions.text: It's said to be dull and commonplace

parts.words: It's said to be dull and commonplace
parts.note: describes a trite remark: something that is spoken aloud and is flat and ordinary

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a thing by reputation as tedious and ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's said' looks like 'people say', but the thing is literally said: a trite remark is uttered and is dull.
explanation.definitionFit: A trite remark is a hackneyed saying repeated so often it has lost all interest.

clue.text: A chore for an' old poet

indicators.note: read as 'exchanged for', so the letters of the first words are traded for a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A tiresome task set for an elderly versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times of this era often signalled anagrams lightly: 'for' says the letters of A CHORE are swapped round. Horace was a Roman lyric poet of the first century BC.
explanation.definitionFit: Quintus Horatius Flaccus was a Latin lyric poet of Augustus's reign, ancient and so 'old'.

clue.text: Out of it — certainly not !

parts.note: the idiom 'out of the ___' means utterly impossible, so the thing you are out of when refusing is the missing word

explanation.surface: Someone rejects an idea indignantly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of it' reads as dazed, but the clue completes the phrase 'out of the question', meaning certainly not.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'out of the question' means not to be considered at all; the missing noun is the clue's 'it'.

clue.text: Even the most fancied can make a backward step

definitions.text: Even the most fancied can make a backward step

parts.words: Even the most fancied can make a backward step
parts.note: the most fancied runners in a race can still fall back and lose

explanation.surface: Even top contenders can slip back.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, the 'fancied' horses are those tipped to win; even they can lose ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Horses or teams most fancied by punters are those expected to win.

clue.text: They're involved in shady transactions

parts.note: shady is read literally as dealing in shades, the colours a cloth-colourer works with

explanation.surface: Crooks are mixed up in dubious deals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady' suggests crookedness, but here it means dealing in shades of colour, the trade of those who colour cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Tradespeople who colour fabric work all day in tints and hues.

clue.text: It records what some people get up to

definitions.text: It records what some people get up to

parts.words: It records what some people get up to
parts.note: get up to is read literally as the height climbers or fliers reach, which an instrument registers

explanation.surface: A device that logs people's mischief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get up to' suggests mischief, but it means the height reached by aviators or mountaineers, which a height gauge records.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft or climber's instrument measures height above sea level.

clue.text: Not an appropriate name for a man-of-war

definitions.text: Not an appropriate name for a man-of-war

parts.words: Not an appropriate name for a man-of-war
parts.note: a warship would hardly be named after the act of ending conflict, Thackeray's middle name

explanation.surface: A warship given an unsuitable name.
explanation.walkthrough: A man-of-war is a warship. William Makepeace Thackeray's middle name means 'bring about peace', hardly fitting for a fighting vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A name meaning to end hostilities, famous as Thackeray's middle name, unsuited to a battleship.

clue.text: Presses on, in a way, with the answers

indicators.note: means arranged in a different manner, so the letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone continues regardless while giving replies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a way' looks like 'to some extent', but signals rearranging the letters of PRESSES ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Replies are what one gives back to questions or calls.

clue.text: With which the geologist may clean up fourteen pounds?

definitions.text: With which the geologist may clean up fourteen pounds?

parts.note: to soap something is to wash it
a stone is a British unit of weight equal to fourteen pounds

explanation.surface: A geologist scrubs up a heavy specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds. The answer is a soft mineral, also called steatite, which feels soapy, so the geologist's 'cleaning' is the soap in its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Steatite is a soft talc-rich rock a geologist would study, named for its greasy, slippery feel.

clue.text: Oft proclaims the man, said Polonius

definitions.text: Oft proclaims the man, said Polonius

parts.words: Oft proclaims the man, said Polonius
parts.note: completes Polonius's advice to Laertes in Hamlet: 'the ___ oft proclaims the man'

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean character offers a proverb about character.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, Polonius tells his son: 'For the ___ oft proclaims the man.'
explanation.definitionFit: Clothing, the dress by which a person's station is judged.

clue.text: Wells character sleeps soundly

indicators.note: read as 'by sound', telling us the word for sleeps is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to kip is British slang for to sleep

explanation.surface: A figure in an H. G. Wells novel is a deep sleeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like it describes deep sleep, but it means 'in sound': KIPS (British slang for sleeps) sounds like the title hero of Wells's 1905 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Kipps is the draper's assistant who inherits a fortune in the H. G. Wells novel named after him.

clue.text: One wouldn't expect to buy it for a tanner

definitions.text: One wouldn't expect to buy it for a tanner

parts.words: One wouldn't expect to buy it for a tanner
parts.note: tanner reads as sixpence, but also as a sunbather seeking a tan, who would not want shade

explanation.surface: Something too dear to buy for sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner was a British sixpence coin; but a tanner is also someone sunbathing, who would hardly want a sunshade.
explanation.definitionFit: A light umbrella carried for shade against the sun.

clue.text: They practise at the bar

parts.note: practising at the bar suggests barristers, but the bar meant is the counter of a pub

explanation.surface: Barristers who work in the courts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practise at the bar' is the phrase for barristers, but here the bar is a pub counter, where those who draw beer work.
explanation.definitionFit: Old word for those who draw and serve ale from the barrel in an inn.

clue.text: They might record sporting finishes

parts.note: read both as recordings of races and as the strings stretched across a finishing line

explanation.surface: Video recordings of the end of races.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record' suggests recordings, which fits, but the finishing strings breasted by winning runners also mark the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: Recording media, and the strips stretched across a race's finishing line.

clue.text: He made a banquet of warm water

definitions.text: He made a banquet of warm water

parts.words: He made a banquet of warm water
parts.note: refers to Shakespeare's misanthrope of Athens, who served false friends covered dishes of warm water

explanation.surface: A host served nothing but hot water at a feast.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Timon of Athens the ruined hero invites his flatterers to a feast and uncovers dishes of warm water.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Athenian misanthrope who mocked his false friends with a sham feast.

clue.text: Where one has left in a pair of, spectacles

indicators.note: one piece is set inside the pair standing on either side

parts.note: two round lenses look like a pair of letter O's
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone has left their glasses somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: PORT (left, the sailor's word) goes in OO (a pair of spectacles, drawn as two rings). 'Where one has' leads to the place, the Portuguese city now called Porto.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in Portugal, the place that gives its name to port wine.

clue.text: A fishy measure

parts.note: fishy reads as suspicious, but means a measure used for fish, herrings in particular

explanation.surface: A dubious step taken by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' suggests shady, but it is literal: a Scottish measure for fresh herrings, about 37.5 gallons.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of volume for fresh herrings, traditionally about 37.5 gallons.

clue.text: It just goes round

parts.note: describes a boundary line, which merely encircles a shape

explanation.surface: A thing that spins aimlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes round' suggests spinning, but it means encircling: the outer boundary of a figure.
explanation.definitionFit: The boundary of a closed figure is the line that encloses it.

clue.text: The masses dispense with them, foolish fellows!

indicators.note: means do without, so a run of letters is dropped from the phrase before it

parts.note: taken as written: the four letters at the start of the opening phrase

explanation.surface: The common people reject the fools.
explanation.walkthrough: Run 'The masses' together and remove the letters of 'them' from its start: what is left is the fools.
explanation.definitionFit: Donkeys are proverbially stupid, so the word serves for silly people.

clue.text: Attendant of Bacchus

parts.note: a plain description of the drunken old satyr in the wine god's train

explanation.surface: A follower of the god of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: In classical myth the wine god was attended by a fat, tipsy old satyr who had been his tutor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the old satyr was the tutor and companion of the wine god Dionysus.

clue.text: Pointers the French require at first

indicators.note: says the word for require comes first, wrapping around the French article before its final letter

parts.note: to require is to need
le is French for 'the'

explanation.surface: French people need to be shown directions to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' places NEED first, then LE (French 'the'), then the S of NEEDS: LE sits inside NEEDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Compass and gauge indicators are thin pointed hands.
